summary:
Since 1 September 2025 consensual same-sex conduct is a criminal offence in Burkina Faso. The Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law that day, by unanimous vote in the 71-member unelected chamber, and it took effect immediately. The penalty is two to five years' imprisonment plus a fine. The ban also covers the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has stated that the prison terms of two to five years and fines apply to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. Deportation therefore sits alongside imprisonment as the direct consequence for a visitor, and the minister's wording on "similar practices" is broader than same-sex conduct alone.

The criminal prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code (CPF), approved by the junta's council in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law, and in force from 1 September 2025. Homosexuality had never before been outlawed in Burkina Faso; the country's criminal code previously contained no such offence.

Reporting from 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship among LGBTQ people in the country. As of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the new law had been reported. The law was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space; the military junta has held power since September 2022.

The sources do not address gender markers on identity or travel documents, legal gender recognition, or screening of travellers on the basis of gender presentation. Nothing in the inventory indicates a formal entry or visa bar targeting trans or gender-nonconforming visitors; the stated risk to a foreign national is prosecution and deportation under the criminal provision.
tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso is among roughly 22 of 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations, placing it within a continental pattern of criminalisation rather than outside it.

The 2025 code overturned an equal age of consent that had been in place since 1996, so the legal position of adults engaging in consensual same-sex relations changed from lawful to criminal within a single legislative instrument.

Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman and describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection; it does not authorise same-sex marriage. The same article bars discrimination in marriage on grounds of race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin or wealth, a list that omits sexual orientation and gender identity, so no constitutional non-discrimination protection covers those characteristics.

Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption remain in force, and the amended family code draft circulated under the Traoré junta in July 2024 targeted consensual same-sex relations before the criminal ban took effect.
localsOnly:
Under the adoption rules reported by the U.S. Department of State, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married for at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

A 2011 U.S. Department of State human rights report found that national law did not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT people were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse, and religious and traditional beliefs did not accept homosexuality. The report found no evidence that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them.

LGBTQ organisations have no legal presence in the country but have operated unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

National adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% among those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% receive antiretroviral drugs, while 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, gender markers on passports or national identity documents, or any document-inspection practice at ports of entry. Whether a visitor's documents could prompt questioning is unresolved on this record.

No source addresses whether the criminal provision has been used against foreign nationals, or how deportation would be carried out in practice; the ministerial statement on deportation is the only sourced basis for that risk.

The enforcement picture is unresolved beyond 28 September 2025: the inventory records no arrests under the law up to that date but contains no later reporting, so current enforcement levels are not sourced.

The discrimination and violence findings are drawn from a 2011 report and predate the 2025 criminalisation; their current accuracy is not verified by anything in the inventory.

Nothing in the inventory is sourced on hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions covering gender identity, on access to legal gender-affirming care, or on whether the criminal ban affects the operation of health services.
